title: How Does a Jet Engine Work?
hook: Most of the air in this modern jet engine never touches the fire.

scenes.label: THE SECRET
scenes.line: Most of the air passing through this modern jet engine never even touches the fire. So where does all that incredible thrust actually come from?

scenes.label: THE GIANT FAN
scenes.line: First, the giant front fan pulls air inside. Much of that air travels through a wide outer passage, bypassing the hot engine core entirely.

scenes.label: SQUEEZE THE AIR
scenes.line: The remaining air enters the core, where several compressor stages squeeze it to a much higher pressure before any fuel is burned.

scenes.label: CONTINUOUS FIRE
scenes.line: Fuel mixes with compressed air inside the combustion chamber and burns continuously. The resulting hot, high energy gas rushes toward the back of the engine.

scenes.label: POWER FROM GAS
scenes.line: As the gas passes through turbine blades, it makes them spin. Shafts carry this energy forward, driving the compressor and the enormous front fan.

scenes.label: THE THRUST
scenes.line: That fan accelerates a huge mass of air backward, while the hot core exhaust adds thrust too. The reaction pushes the aircraft forward. Follow for more engineering.

title: How Do Giant Tunnel Boring Machines Work?
hook: This enormous machine can build a tunnel while digging it.

scenes.label: A MOVING FACTORY
scenes.line: Imagine a machine so enormous it can carve a passage through the ground and help build the tunnel walls as it goes. Here's how it works.

scenes.label: CUTTERHEAD
scenes.line: At the very front, a rotating cutterhead presses specially designed tools into the ground. Different cutters are used for different types of rock and soil.

scenes.label: REMOVE THE SPOIL
scenes.line: All that excavated material has to go somewhere. Depending on the machine, conveyors carry it backward, or fluid carries it away through a pipeline.

scenes.label: PUSH FORWARD
scenes.line: Powerful hydraulic jacks push the machine forward. On many shield machines, those jacks push against the concrete tunnel rings that have already been installed.

scenes.label: BUILD THE WALL
scenes.line: Behind the cutterhead, a mechanical erector positions precast concrete segments into a ring. The segments are joined to form the tunnel's protective lining.

scenes.label: REPEAT
scenes.line: The cycle repeats: cut, remove material, move forward, and build another ring. The exact system changes with the geology. Follow for more engineering.

title: How Do Spacecraft Survive Reentry?
hook: A returning spacecraft faces an extreme heating problem.

scenes.label: THE HOT RETURN
scenes.line: A spacecraft returning from orbit is moving incredibly fast. As it enters denser layers of the atmosphere, the air ahead is forced to change suddenly.

scenes.label: HOT GAS
scenes.line: A powerful shock wave forms in front of the vehicle. The air behind that shock becomes extremely hot, creating a serious challenge for the spacecraft.

scenes.label: HEAT SHIELD
scenes.line: A specially designed heat shield protects the crew or sensitive equipment. It limits how much heat can travel from the outside into the spacecraft.

scenes.label: TWO STRATEGIES
scenes.line: Some heat shields deliberately shed material as they heat, carrying energy away. Other spacecraft use reusable insulating surfaces, including specialized thermal protection tiles.

scenes.label: SLOW DOWN
scenes.line: Meanwhile, atmospheric drag slows the spacecraft and removes much of its kinetic energy. The shape of the vehicle helps control the heating and deceleration.

scenes.label: SAFE DESCENT
scenes.line: The protection system is chosen for the mission, speed, and vehicle design. It is far more than a simple sheet of metal. Follow for more engineering.

title: How Do Submarines Control Their Depth?
hook: A submarine changes its buoyancy on purpose.

scenes.label: SINK ON PURPOSE
scenes.line: How can a huge submarine deliberately sink, then return to the surface? The trick is carefully controlling buoyancy and the forces acting on the vessel.

scenes.label: FLOOD THE TANKS
scenes.line: To dive from the surface, seawater enters the main ballast tanks while air escapes. That changes the submarine's overall weight without changing its outer shape very much.

scenes.label: TRIM THE BOAT
scenes.line: Smaller trim tanks help balance the submarine from front to back. Operators adjust the water inside to fine tune buoyancy and keep the boat level.

scenes.label: STEER UNDERWATER
scenes.line: When the submarine is moving, its diving planes produce hydrodynamic forces, much like underwater wings. Those forces help change its depth and angle.

scenes.label: COME BACK UP
scenes.line: To regain buoyancy for surfacing, compressed air can push seawater back out of the main ballast tanks. The submarine then becomes more buoyant.

scenes.label: A CONTROLLED BALANCE
scenes.line: Buoyancy, trim, forward speed, and control surfaces work together throughout a dive. It takes precise control, not just opening one valve. Follow for more engineering.

title: How Do Tower Cranes Grow Taller?
hook: Some tower cranes can help lift themselves higher.

scenes.label: A SELF CLIMBING CRANE
scenes.line: Look at a tower crane rising alongside a skyscraper. How does it get taller when its own tower is already supporting the entire crane?

scenes.label: MAKE ROOM
scenes.line: Many models use a special climbing frame and powerful hydraulic jacks. The system carefully raises the upper assembly, creating a temporary gap in the tower.

scenes.label: INSERT A SECTION
scenes.line: A new steel mast section is brought into that gap. The crane or a dedicated handling device positions the section for installation.

scenes.label: SECURE THE JOINT
scenes.line: Workers precisely align and secure the new mast section, following the manufacturer's engineered procedure. Every connection must be completed before the system continues.

scenes.label: CLIMB AGAIN
scenes.line: The climbing frame resets and the process can repeat with another section. That lets the crane increase its height in carefully controlled stages.

scenes.label: STAY STABLE
scenes.line: Very tall cranes may also need engineered ties connecting them to the building. Their configuration depends on the crane and site. Follow for more engineering.

title: How Do Flight Recorders Survive Crashes?
hook: An aircraft black box is built to protect its memory.

scenes.label: NOT ACTUALLY BLACK
scenes.line: An aircraft black box is usually bright orange, not black. That bold color is designed to make the recorder easier to locate after an accident.

scenes.label: SAVE THE DATA
scenes.line: Flight data recorders store information about the aircraft. Cockpit voice recorders preserve audio. Their crash protected memory is the most important part to recover.

scenes.label: IMPACT PROTECTION
scenes.line: That memory is surrounded by a rugged protective enclosure built to withstand specified impact and crushing tests. The outer device can still be damaged.

scenes.label: FIRE AND HEAT
scenes.line: Special insulation and protective materials help keep the memory safe through intense fire and heat for specified periods. It is engineering for extreme conditions.

scenes.label: UNDERWATER
scenes.line: Many recorders also have an underwater locator beacon. When activated by contact with water, it sends acoustic pings to help search crews find it.

scenes.label: FIND THE ANSWERS
scenes.line: After a crash, investigators recover the protected memory and analyze the recordings. No recorder is indestructible, but these safeguards improve the chance of finding answers.
